belief: If my child struggles, it's my fault.
origins: Parents often feel responsible for everything that happens to their children. When a child struggles with anxiety, school, friends, behavior, or faith, we search our own parenting for the cause. Well-meaning advice and a misreading of verses about training children can add to the weight.
teaches: Scripture says, “A son will not bear the iniquity of his father, and a father will not bear the iniquity of his son.” “Each of us will give an account of himself to God.” Children are individuals with their own will, temperament, and choices. Proverbs says, “Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.” That is a general principle of wise living, not a guarantee, and not a measure of a parent’s worth. The father in Jesus’ story of the prodigal son did nothing wrong, and yet his son left. When his son came back, “his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him.”
self_statements: If I had been a better parent, they would not struggle.
It is all because of what I did.
I should have seen this coming.
It is my job to fix everything.
errors: Taking responsibility for things beyond my control.
Judging past choices by what I know now.
Believing good parenting guarantees a good outcome.
questions: What factors beyond me contribute, such as temperament, friends, biology, or choices?
Has my child made decisions that are their own?
What real mistakes, if any, can I own without taking all the blame?
What does the father in the prodigal son story teach me?
What does my child need from me now?
What can I trust God with?
truth: I influence my children, but I do not control them. Some of what they face is not my fault, and some may be mine to own and repair. I can love them, take responsibility for what is mine, and trust God with the rest.
hw_truths: My child is responsible for their own choices.
I am not the cause of everything.
I can own real mistakes and repair them.
A loving father runs to meet a returning child.
God cares for my child more than I do.
I can trust God with what I cannot control.
log: Each week, write one thing that is mine to do and one thing you will release to God.
actions: List what is yours to own and what is not.
If there is a real mistake, apologize without excuses or self-punishment.
Spend one-on-one time with your child without fixing.
Pray by name, entrusting them to God each day.
prayer: Lord, I carry my child’s struggles as my own guilt. Show me what is mine to own and what is not. Help me love them well and trust them to You. Amen.
hw_questions: What factors beyond me are involved?
What does my child need now?
name_example: Sarah can write: “Each person answers to God, so I do not carry what is not mine.”
meta: Christian belief counseling for “If my child struggles, it's my fault.” with BSB scriptures, questions, songs, and practical homework.
